title: Once, If I Remember Correctly
text:
«Once, if I remember correctly, my life was a feast where every heart opened, where every wine flowed.


One night, I sat Beauty on my knees. —And I found her bitter.— And I insulted her.


I armed myself against justice.


And I fled. Oh witches, oh misery, oh hatred; only to you was my treasure entrusted!


I managed to banish every human hope from my mind. Over every joy, to strangle it, I carried out the muffled assault of the savage beast.


I called the executioners so I could die biting the butt of their rifles. I invoked plagues to suffocate me with sand, with blood. Misfortune was my god. I hurled myself against the mud. The air of crime dried me out. I played tricks on madness.


And spring gave me the frightful laughter of the idiot.


But now, recently, when I was about to breathe my last, I thought of seeking the key to the old feast, at which, perhaps, I would regain my appetite.


Charity is that key. —That inspired assertion proves that I have been dreaming!


«You will remain a hyena, etc…» declares the demon who crowned me with such pleasant poppies. «Earn your death with all your appetites, and with your selfishness and all the deadly sins».


Ah! I have endured enough: —But, dear Satan, I beg you, do not be so angry with me! And while I await those little vile acts I still have left to commit, I detach for you, who love in the writer the absence of every descriptive or instructive faculty, a few disgusting pages from my notebook of the condemned.




A Season in Hell, 1873
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Rimbaud's French original. The stray line break before the comma in the source's closing publication line is repaired; the translation preserves the quoted voices, reversals, and grotesque imagery.

title: Ophelia
text:
I

In the deep waters that rock the stars,

white and innocent, Ophelia floats like a great lily,

so slowly she floats, reclining in her veils…

when the death knell sounds in the distant forest.


For thousands of years now pale Ophelia

passes, a white ghost, along the great black river;

for more than a thousand years her gentle madness

murmurs its tune in the night air.


The wind, like a corolla, caresses her breasts

and unfurls, rocked, its blue sail;

the trembling willows weep against her shoulders

and over her dreaming brow the cattail bends.


The curled water lilies sigh beside her,

while she awakens, in the sleeping alder,

a nest from which a tiny tremor rises…

and a song, all gold, falls from the mysterious sky.


II


Oh most sorrowful Ophelia, beautiful as snow,

dead when you were a child, carried away by the river!

For the cold winds falling from Norway

had whispered austere freedom to you.


And an arcane breath, as it shook your hair,

put strange voices into your dazed mind;

and your heart listened to the lament

of Nature—the sound of trees and nights.


And the voice of the sea, like an immense gasp,

broke your mild and tender child's heart;

and one April day, a beautiful pale child,

a wretched madman, sat down at your feet.


Heaven, Love, Freedom: what a dream, oh poor Madwoman!

You melted into it like snow into fire;

your visions, immense, drowned your speech.

—And terrible Infinity frightened your blue eye.


III


And the poet tells us that on the starry night

you come to gather the flowers you picked,

and that he has seen, reclining in your veils,

the innocent Ophelia floating like a great lily in the water.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Rimbaud's French original. The three-part structure and the source's changing lily terms are rendered as the recurring lily image, with the dreamlike ambiguities retained.

title: The Poor in Church
text:
Parked on oak benches, in the corners
of the church that warms its breath, their eyes
fixed on the gilded choir, while the choir
roars pious songs from their throats,
inhaling wax like the smell of a loaf,
happy, humiliated, like beaten dogs,
the Good Lord's poor, the patron and master,
offer their Oremuses, ridiculous and obtuse.


It is fine to offer smooth benches to the female
after the six days in which God mistreats her!
for she rocks, wrapped in strange furs,
something akin to a child that cries without cease.


With filthy breasts in the open air, these soup women,
with prayer clinging to eyes that do not pray,
look at the little hussies with their sad display,
seekers beneath the brim of the deformed hat.


Outside, the cold and hunger and the man with his revelry:
well, then! one hour more; afterward, a thousand ills.
—Meanwhile, all around them, a little group of old women
with enormous double chins moans, drones, chatters.


And there are the epileptics and those terrified ones
whom everyone flees at the crossroads;
and, happily sniffing old missals,
those blind men whom a dog leads into the courtyards.


Drooling a beggarly and stupid faith,
they all tell their endless complaint to Jesus,
who dreams above, pallid in the yellow light,
far from thin sinners and potbellied sinners,


from the smell of flesh and moldy cloth:
humble, gloomy farce of disgusting gestures.
—And prayer blooms with chosen phrases,
and mysticism takes on urgent shades,


when the sun dies in the nave, and bland folds of silk,
dull green laughter, the ladies of distinguished neighborhoods,
—Jesus!—the liver-sick women,
offer their fingers to be kissed in the holy water.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Rimbaud's French original. The harsh social register and bodily grotesquerie are retained; the source's odd 'comacas' comparison is rendered as the clear little-dog image without importing a different scene.

title: To Music
text:
In the square outlined by a sparse, poor lawn,
and where everything is proper, flowers, trees,
the panting bourgeois, choking in the heat,
bring their stupidity every Thursday night.

—The military band, in the middle of the garden,
to the Fife Waltz, rocks the shako:
—the dandy displays himself in the front rows
and the notary is nothing but the trinkets hanging from him.


Monocled rentiers underline the mistakes:
puffed-up bureaucrats drag their ladies,
beside whom run, faithful as little dogs,
women in flounces that look like advertisements.


Seated on the benches, retired shopkeepers,
as they prod the sand with their canes,
discuss treaties with great dignity,
snuff silver snuff, and continue: «Well, we were saying!…»


Flattening a plump, flabby back against his bench,
a bourgeois with silver buttons and a northern belly
savors his pipe, from which a strand
of tobacco falls; —You know, I buy it on the black market.


And across the green lawn the young rascals laugh,
while, in love with the sound of the trombone,
innocent, the little bandsmen, sniffing a rose,
caress the child, thinking of the nanny…


I go on, a wreck, just like a student,
beneath the horse chestnut, toward the merry girls:
they know it and turn toward me, laughing,
their eyes curdled with indiscreet ideas.


I do not say a word, but I look at the flesh
of their white, embroidered necks, beneath mad curls:
and I follow the curve, under the light corset,
of a goddess's back, beyond the shoulder's arch.


Soon, like a greyhound, I stalk boots, stockings…
—I reconstruct the bodies and burn in beautiful fevers.
They find me strange and go whispering…
—My brutal desires catch on their lips…
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Rimbaud's French original. The apparent source corruption 'comacas' is repaired to the evident small-dog comparison, and the colloquial 'turutas' is rendered as little bandsmen; the satire and erotic gaze remain intact.

title: Oh You Who Lie Beneath the Earth, O Sorrowful People
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. The arrow metals, repeated war imagery, and formal address are preserved; archaic syntax is lightly smoothed only where English requires it.

title: No More Than the Clear Fountain
text:
No more than the clear fountain
does a wounded deer desire,
do I, your surrendered one,
desire always to be before you.
To the great and sweet rest
where my contentment lies,
I feel no other bridge
to find another passage, nor dare.


The day comes late,
so greatly desired by me,
bought at a very dear price
with my pain and sorrow.


But at last, late or early,
I am certain it must come,
unless death closes the road
that it has opened with its hand.


I cannot be cast out of hope
under any circumstance,
for, lady, I have loved you
according to blessedness.


And favored by you,
I feel nothing against me,
if your consent grants me
what I ask of you.


I feel a mountain of great pains
set before me,
of a thousand obstacles
that have opposed my contentment.


I fear to ask you for news of me,
lady, doubting that there is love
for me put to the test.


And I fear not knowing it,
living in greater torment,
and with these two pains I feel
I burn whichever way I turn.


It is not in you to content yourself
with fulfilling what I ask,
even if you wish to force yourself
against yourself, as a bargain.


Love, love is what must advise you
so that my good may be fulfilled
in you and in it.


Let nothing make you fear
that you will receive offense;
my thoughts have given
the truth its own color.


That serving you will have been
confirmed in steadfastness;
in this kind of service
love wishes to be served.


If this language you hear
seems a lie to you,
either you live without love
or you do not know what it wants.


He who feels this torment
can hardly rest;
only in movement
will you have a safe place.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. The courtly plea, bridge and mountain obstacles, and final paradox of movement and safety are retained.

title: The Tongue Cannot Express the Great Pain
text:
The tongue cannot express the great pain
of one who, dying, does not know where he will go
(whether God will want to keep him beside Him
or whether He will want to bury him in hell):
such pain my spirit feels,
for not knowing what He has ordained for you,
since your good or evil has been given to me,
and whatever happens to you, I will suffer.


Spirit, oh you who have already left
that body I loved so much,
look at me sunk in affliction
and doubting whether to speak to you sanely.
The place where you are will overturn
the meaning of everything I have to say;
through you I will gain sorrow or joy:
whatever God wishes to give me is found in you.


I will not clasp my hands to pray,
for its destiny is already fulfilled:
indescribable is its good, if it is in Heaven;
if in Hell, my praying is in vain.
If that is so, may my spirit annihilate itself,
and God return my being to nothing,
especially if it is there because of me.
Let it not be I who suffer such great harm.


I know how to say nothing I have not said;
whether I shout or keep silent, nothing satisfies me;
whether I wander or think, time is consumed,
and before doing things I repent.
I do not lament the pain of vanished pleasure—
so much fear does its great evil cause me!
The evil that is not perpetual is a slight evil,
but I fear this one has not been earned.


The harm of death terrifies,
and being treated equally diminishes it.
Oh pain, be impartial to me,
and be protection against oblivion!
Strike my heart and senses,
gorge yourself on me, for I do not defend myself,
cause me so much harm that I become pitiable.
Let your power encompass me as fully as it can.


Spirit, if nothing prevents you,
break the common custom of the dead;
return to the world and tell me what has become of you:
your gaze will not frighten me.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. The poem's theological uncertainty, direct apostrophe to the dead spirit, and desire for pain against oblivion are kept without resolving its paradoxes.

title: What Sure Counsel Are You Seeking?
text:
What sure counsel are you seeking,
unhappy heart, sick of living?
Friend of tears and enemy of laughter,
how will you bear the evils awaiting you?
Hasten, then, toward the death that awaits you,
though to your harm you prolong your days;
the farther away your delightful dwelling lies,
the more you want to flee inciting death.
With open arms she comes out onto the road,
her eyes weeping from an excess of joy;
I hear the melodious song of her voice,
which says: «Friend, leave another's house.
I take pleasure in giving you my favor,
which no man born has ever had,
for I flee the one who calls me,
taking only the one who flees my rigor.»


With her eyes weeping, her face terrified,
tearing her hair with great cries,
life wants to give me inheritances,
and the lord of these gifts wants me to be,
shouting with a horrible, painful voice,
as death calls the blessed;
for to one accustomed to suffering,
the voice of death will be melodious.


How the proud
will of so many lovers amazes me!
Without even asking me what Love is,
they will find its painful strength in me.
Cursing, they will all swear
that Love will never possess them,
but if I speak to them of warm pleasure,
they will curse lost time, sighing.


I know no man or woman like me
who, tormented by Love, inspires pity;
I am the one to be pitied,
for the blood withdraws from my heart.
Because of the sadness that approached it,
the humor that sustains my life dried forever;
against me sadness shows its boldness,
and no armed hand comes to my aid.


Lily among thorns, I feel the hour approaching
when my life is civilly concluded;
since my hope is entirely lost,
my soul remains condemned in this world.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. Death and life remain personified as competing speakers, and the source's strange inheritance and 'civilly concluded' phrasing are retained.

title: Let People Seek Festivities with Joy
text:
Let people seek festivities with joy,
praising God and mingling sports;
let squares, streets, and delightful gardens
fill with the tales of great deeds;
and let me go searching for tombs,
questioning condemned souls,
who will answer me, since they are accompanied
only by me in their perpetual lament.


Each person seeks and wants his like;
for this reason the company of the living does not please me.
When they imagine my state, they turn evasive;
as from a dead man, they take fright at me.
The Cyprian king, prisoner of a heretic,
is not unfortunate in my eyes,
for what I want will never be achieved;
no physician can cure my desire.


Like Prometheus, whose liver the eagle eats
and whose flesh always grows again,
and the bird's devouring never ends;
a pain stronger than this has besieged me,
for one worm gnaws my thought,
another my heart, and they never stop gnawing,
and their work can be interrupted
only by what is impossible to achieve.


And if death did not inflict the offense
of taking me from so pleasant a vision,
I would not thank it for clothing in earth
my naked body, I who do not think to lose
pleasure, since I only imagine
that my desires cannot be fulfilled;
and if my final hour has arrived,
the end of loving well will arrive too.


And if God wishes to shelter me in heaven,
in addition to seeing Him, to fulfill my desire
it will be necessary that I be told there
that you are pleased to mourn my death,
repenting that through your scant mercy
an innocent died, a martyr for loving you:
for I would separate body from soul
if I truly believed that it pained you.


Lily among thorns, you know and I know
that one may well die for love;
if you believe I am in such pain,
you will not go too far in placing full faith in it.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. The cemetery dialogue, Prometheus image, and conditional hope of heavenly proof remain unresolved as in the Spanish source.

title: To My Fate I Entrust My Affairs
text:
To my fate I entrust my affairs,
for I have already been separated from my choice;
my reason is dead and its excesses alive,
since it abandoned me at the beginning;
I will no longer hold my desires captive,
my good will is sick today;
I go where thought would not want to go,
discontent with everything I can do.


Like the crippled paralytic
who, set on his feet, cannot take a step,
but you see him fall despite himself
and his will is fulfilled in nothing,
so am I, for I do what I have not wanted;
reason overcomes desire, and if it pleases
I will lose pleasure and receive the payment,
for without a heart I do all you see me do.


Just as a ship gives itself to the winds
and, while battling against them,
its sad, discontented sailors
let it go where it wishes and it runs,
so are my reason and my feelings now,
fighting the body's desire;
they dare not decide who moves it,
and appetite carries it where it goes.


The time has passed when I was content,
and I always felt its sour taste,
contentment mixed with pain;
I thought myself a king, finding myself its slave;
in its ills without goods I made my home,
although no evil without good ever came to an end;
for them I considered dying a good thing:
he lives badly who does not put a brake on doing evil.


Oh you, Love, who extend your power
so far that I cannot resist you!
Come out of me now, say what you intend,
for my will flees from serving you.
You kindle your great pride against me;
let live the one who will not serve you:
what movement overcomes the evil I have,
since I break away from this false love?


This deed of mine shows no good ending,
and the present is full of sadness;
I am not satisfied with the future,
for I already clearly feel its harm;
I shall surely suffer it if the woman I love
sees the harm my soul feels,
and without repenting in any way,
then I shall have pleasure even with death.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Ausiàs March's Catalan original. The conflict of reason, will, body, ship, and appetite is preserved, along with the poem's deliberately archaic turns.

title: Ballad of the Forester and the Countess
text:
In the lands of Sweden lived a countess
who was so pale and so beautiful.
«Sir forester, sir forester, my garter has come loose,
has come loose, come loose!
Forester, kneel down, quickly, and tie it for me!»


«Lady countess, lady countess, do not look at me so,
I serve you for my bread.
Your breasts are white, but the axe is cold,
is cold, is cold!
Sweet is love, but bitter is death.»


The forester escaped that same night.
He rode down the mountain until he reached the sea.
«Sir boatman, sir boatman, take me into your boat,
into your boat, into your boat!
Boatman, I must go to the end of the sea.»
Between the cock and the fox, love sprang forth.
«Oh golden one, do you love me truly?»
and the night was fine, but dawn arrived,
arrived, arrived:
all its feathers hang from the bramble.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The repeated calls, the counterpoint of white breasts and cold axe, and the final dawn image are preserved.

title: Song of a Beloved
text:
1. I know it, beloved: now my hair falls out from my wild life,
and I lie on the stones. You see me drink the cheapest schnapps,
and I walk naked in the wind.


2. But there was a time, beloved, when I was pure.


3. I had a woman who was stronger than I, as grass
is stronger than the bull: it rises again.


4. She saw that I was bad, and she loved me.


5. She did not ask where the road led, which was her road,
and perhaps went downward. When she gave me her body, she said:
this is all. And it was my body.


6. Now she is nowhere, she disappeared like a cloud when it has rained,
I abandoned her and she fell, for that was her road.


7. But at night, sometimes, when you see me drink, I see her face,
pale in the wind, strong and turned toward me, and I bow before the wind.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The numbered fragments, the grass-and-bull comparison, and the final ambiguity of bowing to the wind are retained.

title: Four Love Songs
text:
I
When, later, I went away from you
into the enormous today,
I saw, when I began to see,
cheerful and decent people.


And from that late hour,
you know which one I mean,
I have a more beautiful mouth
and more agile legs.


Since then there is more green
in tree, branch, and meadow,
and the water is fresher
when I pour it over myself.


II
When you make me have
such a good time, I sometimes think:
if I died now
I would have been happy
to the end.


When you are old
and remember me,
think of me as I am today
and you will have a love
that remains young.


III
There are seven roses in the bouquet,
six the wind carries away,
one remains for me
to find.


I called you seven times,
six times you did not answer,
on the seventh, promise
that you will say something to me.


IV
My beloved gave me a branch
with yellow leaves.


The year is coming to an end
and love is beginning.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The four-part sequence, the source's unusual 'enormous today,' and the numerical repetitions are preserved.
